name: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome/Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis Overlap Syndrome

criteria.description: Epidermal detachment involving 10-30% of body surface area
Involvement of at least two mucous membranes (oral, ocular, genital)
Skin biopsy showing full-thickness epidermal necrosis
Fever and flu-like prodrome preceding skin lesions

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of epidermal detachment involving 10-30% BSA plus mucosal involvement in at least two sites
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is clinical and supported by histopathology; drug history is critical for identifying causative agents.

pathognomonic.notes: Characteristic skin sloughing differentiates overlap syndrome from isolated SJS or TEN
searchTerms: large areas of skin sloughing off

pathognomonic.symptomName: Bilateral conjunctival inflammation with mucosal erosions
searchTerms: both eyes red with mucous membrane sores

pathognomonic.symptomName: Painful mucosal erosions involving oral and genital mucosa
searchTerms: painful sores in mouth and genital areas
fever and feeling unwell before rash
flu-like symptoms prior to skin rash
malaise and fever before rash onset

common.symptomName: Targetoid macules and atypical target lesions
Dysphagia due to oropharyngeal mucosal involvement
searchTerms: throat mucosa involvement with swallowing problems

occasional.symptomName: Respiratory distress due to bronchial mucosal involvement
searchTerms: respiratory distress due to bronchial swelling

rare.symptomName: Sepsis secondary to skin barrier loss
searchTerms: blood infection due to skin barrier loss

laboratory: Electrolyte imbalances due to fluid loss
imaging: Chest X-ray may show infiltrates if respiratory involvement present
genetic: HLA-B*1502 allele associated with increased risk in some Asian populations
other: Skin biopsy demonstrating full-thickness epidermal necrosis with subepidermal bullae

distinguishingFeatures: Chronic course vs acute onset in SJS/TEN
Absence of systemic symptoms like fever
Target lesions without extensive epidermal detachment
Usually associated with infections rather than drugs

redFlags: Rapid progression of skin detachment over >10% body surface area
Signs of sepsis or multi-organ failure
Severe ocular involvement risking permanent vision loss
references: Schwartz RA, McDonough PH, Lee BW. Toxic epidermal necrolysis: Part I. Introduction, history, classification, clinical features, systemic manifestations, etiology, and immunopathogenesis. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2013;69(2):173.e1-13.
Roujeau JC, Stern RS. Severe adverse cutaneous reactions to drugs. N Engl J Med. 1994;331(19):1272-85.
RegiSCAR Group. Validation of the SCAR criteria for Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. Clin Exp Dermatol. 2007;32(5):512-6.
